r3-fix verification:
- Encoder corpus. The r3 corpus (2071 cases) and a new adversarial corpus (3428 cases) were checked byte-for-byte. The new corpus covers each lead byte 0xc2..0xff directly before every special (\\, ", \n, \r, \t, 0x01..0x1f, 0x7f) and straddling the 256-byte boundary. It also covers truncated and continuation sequences, every CTLESC/CTLNUL/backslash/quote/ESC triple, and glob metacharacters mixed with random soup. Both corpora give 0 mismatches and 0 stderr under LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, C and POSIX, with BASH_COMPAT default, 32 and 42, and with the Bash 3.2 printf -v shim. Each case is fed through argv (scripts/enc-argv.py). A first harness that stripped a sentinel with ${s%x} in the caller showed mismatches. They came from the same Bash 5.2 bug in the harness's own expansion, not from the encoder: minimal repro s=$'\\\\\\\xe0\\\xe0\\\\x'; ${s%x} under C.UTF-8 -> 5c 5c 5c 62 54 56.
- local LC_ALL=C. It takes effect inside the function and the locale is restored on return, even when the function is called directly (no subshell), under LC_ALL, LANG or LC_CTYPE=C.UTF-8 and BASH_COMPAT 32/42/50 (scripts/loc-scope.sh). ${#1} and ${s:pos:256} are both computed in C, so chunking stays consistent.
- Consumer-style messages (emoji with VS16, ANSI ESC, \x01\x7f, quotes and backslashes, the jq-missing text, invalid UTF-8) through sb_emit_hook_message, _decision, _context and Stop block, with no jq and no python3: 28 documents per configuration, all valid and exact, in C.UTF-8 and C, default and BASH_COMPAT=32. Invalid UTF-8 passes through raw from the Bash encoder, as documented, pre-existing.
- Performance at load average 20: 64 KB mixed in 1.25 s (C.UTF-8) and 0.85 s (C); 76 KB multibyte in about 1 s.
- The wall-clock assertion is gone; the 64 KB case now asserts exact equality. It passed under coverage instrumentation (test-hook-output took 82 s in the coverage run, 0 failures).

notes: Nits, not issues: (1) the hook-output.sh:58 comment still says '256-character chunks'; in the C locale they are 256-byte chunks, which is fine because output is concatenated bytes. (2) The lead-byte test passes vacuously on a machine without a C.UTF-8 locale (CI Linux has one). Cross-area observation for the orchestrator (outside F1): the Bash 5.2 UTF-8 bug is not specific to the encoder. Any hook that applies ${var%...}, ${var%%...} or ${var#...} to untrusted text containing a lone UTF-8 lead byte followed by a backslash, in a UTF-8 locale, can read uninitialised bytes. See the minimal repro in validation.tests.
